problems.title: Problem 1
problems.problem:
Problem 1 [20 points]

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/poland-2017-1-fig1.png

A uniform cylinder of mass $M$ and radius $R$ was rolling without slipping on a flat floor with speed $v_0$ and struck a uniform cuboid block of mass $m$, initially at rest. The direction of motion of the cylinder was perpendicular to the left face of the block (see the figure). The height of the block is greater than the radius of the cylinder. The cylinder and the block have a common plane of symmetry perpendicular to the floor. The coefficient of friction between the block and the floor is equal to $f_1$, and between the block and the cylinder $f_2$. The collision lasted a very short time, and as its result the components, parallel to the floor, of the velocities of the centres of mass of the cylinder and of the block became equal. The length of the block is so large that the face in contact with the floor does not lift off it.

What conditions must the coefficients of friction $f_1$ and $f_2$ satisfy for the impact considered not to cause a displacement of the block?

The moment of inertia of the cylinder about its axis is $\frac{1}{2}MR^2$. Assume that interactions inside the block, the cylinder and the floor propagate infinitely fast. Neglect rolling friction.

problems.title: Problem 2
problems.problem:
Problem 2 [20 points]

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/poland-2017-2-fig1.png

Between the plates of a parallel-plate capacitor, separated by $2d$ and each of area $S$, there are two layers of different materials, parallel to the plates: material A of electric permittivity $\epsilon_\mathrm{A}$, resistivity $\rho_\mathrm{A}$ and layer thickness $d$, and material B of electric permittivity $\epsilon_\mathrm{B}$, resistivity $\rho_\mathrm{B}$ and layer thickness $d$. The distance between the plates is much smaller than their linear dimensions.

The plates of the capacitor were connected to a battery of electromotive force $\mathcal{E}$ and negligible internal resistance for a very long time, such that the changes of the current flowing in the circuit became unnoticeable.

Then the battery was disconnected, and the plates were short-circuited for a short time with a resistor of resistance much smaller than the resistance of the capacitor, so that the voltage between them dropped to $\mathcal{E}/2$. Determine the dependence of the voltage between the plates of the capacitor on the time elapsed since this resistor was disconnected.

Hint

When the plates of an ideal capacitor of capacitance $C$ are short-circuited with a resistor of resistance $R$, the voltage between these plates changes in time according to the formula

$$U = U_0 e^{-\frac{t}{RC}},$$

where $U_0$ is the initial voltage, and $t$ is the time elapsed since the moment the plates were short-circuited.

problems.title: Problem 3
problems.problem:
Problem 3 [20 points]

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/poland-2017-3-fig1.png

[Labels in the figure: Słońce = Sun; nagrzewnica = heater; zwierciadło = mirror; chłodnica = cooler.]

A solar power station transmitting energy to the Earth by means of a laser beam was placed in outer space.

The power station consists of the following elements:

• an ideal mirror which is a part of a cylindrical surface of radius $R$, length $L$ and width $2r_1$; the mirror is set perpendicular to the direction Sun – power station.
• a heater which is a half-cylinder of length $L$, with an ideally white (non-radiating) curved surface and a perfectly black, perfectly heat-conducting flat surface
• a cylindrical cooler of radius $r_2$ and length $L$, with an ideally black lateral surface and ideally white end faces
• a heat engine taking heat from the heater and giving heat to the cooler; the engine is not shown in the figure, some of its elements may be located inside the heater or the cooler

and additional elements (among others, pipes connecting the heater, the cooler and the engine) which are not essential in the problem considered. The end faces of the cooler and of the heater do not radiate. The temperature of the surface of the Sun is $T_\mathrm{s}$, the radius of the Sun is $R_\mathrm{s}$, the distance centre of the Sun – power station is $d$. The Stefan–Boltzmann constant is denoted by the letter $\sigma$.

a) Determine the radius of the heater $r_\mathrm{n}$ for which (assuming its optimal position) the difference between the amount of energy delivered to it and radiated from it will be the largest.

Below, assume that the radius of the heater is equal to the radius determined in part a), and that its placement is optimal (as in part a).

b) Determine the maximum temperature $T_\mathrm{max}$ that the heater can reach.

c) Determine the maximum theoretically possible efficiency of the engine and the temperature of the cooler at this efficiency. Express the results in terms of $p_\mathrm{s}$ – the power of the solar radiation per unit area near the station (the solar constant), $T_\mathrm{max}$ from part b), $r_1$, $r_2$, $L$, $\sigma$ and $T_1$ – the temperature of the heater.

d) Give the numerical values of the quantities determined for $r_1 = 10\,\mathrm{m}$, $L = 20\,\mathrm{m}$, $R = 20\,\mathrm{m}$, $r_2 = 1\,\mathrm{m}$, $T_1 = 1200\,\mathrm{K}$, $R_\mathrm{s} = 7.0\cdot10^{8}\,\mathrm{m}$, $d = 1.5\cdot10^{11}\,\mathrm{m}$, $T_\mathrm{s} = 5800\,\mathrm{K}$, $\sigma = 5.7\cdot10^{-8}\,\mathrm{W/(m^2K^4)}$.

Note:

Take into account that $R_\mathrm{s}/d \ll 1$, $r_1 < R < R_\mathrm{s}$, $L < R_\mathrm{s}$, and neglect the fact that the heater blocks part of the light falling on the mirror. Neglect also the presence of the mirror near the cooler, the fact that part of the radiation emitted by the heater returns to it after reflection from the mirror, and all external radiation except the radiation of the Sun. Apply the paraxial-ray approximation of geometrical optics.

problems.title: Problem 1
problems.problem:
Problem 1 [20 points]

A rubber band (an office elastic band) is uniform, has the shape of a loop, mass $m$ and free length $2\pi r_0$. The cross-section of the band is a rectangle whose sides are much shorter than $r_0$; the ratio of the lengths of the shorter and the longer side of this rectangle is much smaller than unity. That the spring constant of the band is $k$ means that, after the band is cut and straightened, a force of magnitude $F$ applied along the band stretches the band by a segment of length $\frac{F}{k}$.

The band was placed on a cone with apex angle $2\alpha$, so that it was in contact with the cone through the longer side of its cross-section, always the same one. Then the band was released. The curve running along the band through the centre of its cross-section always formed a circle lying in a plane perpendicular to the axis of the cone. The radius of this circle was initially equal to $r_1$, where $r_1 > r_0$.

Determine the time interval $\Delta t$ from the moment the band is released to the moment when it forms a circle of radius $r_0$. The coefficient of friction between the band and the cone is $\mu$, where $\mathrm{tg}\,\alpha > \mu$. Gravity is to be neglected.

problems.title: Problem 2
problems.problem:
Problem 2 [20 points]

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/poland-2018-2-fig1.png

Figure for Problem 2: the tape before folding, with the fold lines marked. The direction of the current flow is also marked.

A conducting tape consists of many identical, parallel, insulated wires. The width $w$ of this tape is much larger than its thickness, and the distance between neighbouring wires and the thickness of the insulation can be neglected.

The tape was folded through an angle of $180^\mathrm{o}$ along a straight line making an angle of $60^\mathrm{o}$ with the direction of the wires. Then it was folded in the opposite direction through an angle of $180^\mathrm{o}$ along a straight line making an angle of $60^\mathrm{o}$ with the direction of the wires, and this operation was repeated $3n-1$ times in total. The distance between the folds is such that each flat fragment between folds forms an equilateral triangle, called a plate below. The end fragments of the tape were cut off so that equilateral triangles were also formed at the beginning and at the end. As a result, a system of $3n$ parallel fragments in the shape of an equilateral triangle (plates) of height $w$ was formed. The distance between neighbouring plates is $d$ ($d \ll w$).

The ends of the tape were connected to supply leads in such a way that the current of the same intensity flows through every wire forming the tape, i.e. a current of uniform density flows through every plate. The total current is equal to $I$.

Determine the electrodynamic force acting on each of the plates. Neglect the influence of the magnetic field produced by the supply leads. Take the magnetic permeability of the insulation of the wires and the magnetic permeability of air equal to the magnetic permeability of vacuum $\mu_0$.

[Information that may be useful (printed on a separate page for the whole paper):

1. Gauss's law

For the electric field $\vec{E}$ in vacuum, the gravitational field (gravitational acceleration) $\vec{\gamma}$ and the magnetic induction vector $\vec{B}$, the total flux $\varPhi_{\text{całk}}$ of the given field through a closed surface is equal to

$$\varPhi_{\text{całk}} = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{\varepsilon_0}Q & \text{for the electric field,} \\ -4\pi G\cdot M & \text{for the gravitational field,} \\ 0 & \text{for the magnetic field,} \end{cases}$$

where $Q$ is the total electric charge contained inside the surface considered, $M$ the total mass contained inside the surface considered, $\varepsilon_0$ the electric permittivity of vacuum, and $G$ the universal gravitational constant.

$\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\cdot10^{-12}\,\mathrm{F/m}$, $G = 6.67\cdot10^{-11}\,\mathrm{N\cdot m^2/kg^2}$.

2. Magnetic induction of the field produced by a current flowing in a plane

If in the plane $z = 0$ a current of constant linear density $j$ flows along the $x$ axis, in the direction of the axis, then the components of the magnetic induction vector of the field produced by this current are equal to

$$B_y = -\frac{1}{2}\mu_0 j \ \text{ for } z > 0, \quad B_y = +\frac{1}{2}\mu_0 j \ \text{ for } z < 0, \qquad B_x = B_z = 0.$$

The linear density of a current flowing in a plane is the current $I$ flowing in a strip of width $a$ divided by this width, i.e. $j = I/a$.

The above formulas follow from Ampère's law, presented below (in a simplified form).

Ampère's law

The circulation $\mathcal{E}_B$ of the magnetic induction vector $\vec{B}$ along a closed polygonal line W is the quantity

$$\mathcal{E}_B = \sum_{k=1}^{N}\vec{B}_k\cdot\Delta\vec{l}_k,$$

where $\Delta\vec{l}_k$ correspond to the successive segments of the polygonal line W, and $\vec{B}_k$ is the mean magnetic induction vector on the segment $\Delta\bar{l}_k$.

In vacuum, according to Ampère's law, the circulation $\mathcal{E}_B$ of the magnetic induction vector $\vec{B}$ along a closed polygonal line W is equal to the total current $I$ flowing through the surface $S$ whose boundary is the polygonal line W, multiplied by the magnetic permeability of vacuum $\mu_0$:

$$\mathcal{E}_B = \mu_0 I.$$

]

a) Let $v_{0\mathrm{BA}}$ denote the initial speed of a small body launched from point B in the direction of point A. Give the maximal interval of initial speeds to which $v_{0\mathrm{BA}}$ must belong for this body to reach point A in a finite time.

b) Let $v_{0\mathrm{AC}}$ denote the initial speed of a small body launched from point A in the direction of point C. Give the maximal interval of initial speeds to which $v_{0\mathrm{AC}}$ must belong for this body to reach point C in a finite time.

The planet is at rest.

[Information that may be useful (printed on a separate page for the whole paper):

1. Gauss's law

For the electric field $\vec{E}$ in vacuum, the gravitational field (gravitational acceleration) $\vec{\gamma}$ and the magnetic induction vector $\vec{B}$, the total flux $\varPhi_{\text{całk}}$ of the given field through a closed surface is equal to

$$\varPhi_{\text{całk}} = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{\varepsilon_0}Q & \text{for the electric field,} \\ -4\pi G\cdot M & \text{for the gravitational field,} \\ 0 & \text{for the magnetic field,} \end{cases}$$

where $Q$ is the total electric charge contained inside the surface considered, $M$ the total mass contained inside the surface considered, $\varepsilon_0$ the electric permittivity of vacuum, and $G$ the universal gravitational constant.

problems.title: Problem 1
problems.problem:
Problem 1 [20 points]

Two identical resistors 1 and 2 are given, with constant specific heat and with resistance depending on the temperature $T$ according to the formula

$$R = R_0\left(1 + \alpha\,\Delta T\right),$$

where $R_0$ is the resistance at a temperature equal to the ambient temperature $T_0$, $\Delta T = T - T_0$, and $\alpha$ is a positive constant. The rate of heat outflow $\Delta Q/\Delta t$ from each of the resistors to the surroundings is proportional to the temperature difference $\Delta T$:

$$\frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t} = \beta\,\Delta T,$$

where $\beta$ is a certain positive constant.

The resistors were connected in series and connected to a source of constant voltage $U$. We assume that heat flows between each of the resistors and the surroundings, but not between the resistors.

a) If the initial temperatures $T_1$ and $T_2$ of the resistors were slightly higher than $T_0$ and different from each other (assume $T_1 > T_2$), is it possible that the difference of these temperatures started to grow? If so, what condition must the parameters $U$, $R_0$, $\alpha$ and $\beta$ satisfy for this to happen?

b) Is it possible that after a long time, when the temperatures $T_1$ and $T_2$ have become steady, they remain different? If so, what condition must the parameters $U$, $R_0$, $\alpha$ and $\beta$ satisfy for this to happen?

[Formulas that may be useful (printed once for the whole paper): According to the Stefan–Boltzmann law, a perfect black body of surface area $S$ and absolute temperature $T$ emits radiation of power $P = \sigma S T^4$, where $\sigma = 5.7\cdot10^{-8}\,\mathrm{W/\left(m^2K^4\right)}$ is the Stefan–Boltzmann constant. For $|x| \ll 1$: $(1+x)^r \approx 1 + rx$, $\ln(1+x) \approx x$.]

problems.title: Problem 2
problems.problem:
Problem 2 [20 points]

On 12 August 2018 the space probe Parker Solar Probe was launched, intended to study the vicinity of the Sun, including the solar corona. Let us consider "how hot" it is at the distances to which this probe will approach the Sun.

The distance of the probe from the centre of the Sun during the whole time considered is equal to $d$ (where $d \gg R_\mathrm{S}$). Treat the Sun as a spherical perfect black body of radius $R_\mathrm{S}$ and surface temperature $T_\mathrm{S}$. Neglect the solar wind.

A. Assume that the probe is a sphere of radius $r$ with uniform temperature and that it can be treated as a perfect black body.

1. Determine the (absolute) temperature $T_\mathrm{r}$ that the probe would reach after staying for a long time at the distance $d$ from the centre of the Sun.

2. Estimate, to an accuracy of 10%, the time after which the probe would reach the temperature $T_\mathrm{r}/2$ if it were heated uniformly from a temperature close to $0\,\mathrm{K}$. Assume that the density of the material of which the probe is built is constant and equal to $\rho$, while the mean specific heat during the heating is $C$ (according to the third law of thermodynamics the specific heat must decrease to zero as the temperature tends to $0\,\mathrm{K}$; however, since we only want to estimate the heating time, we shall use the mean specific heat here).

B. Suppose that at the same distance $d$ from the centre of the Sun as the probe there is a uniform sphere of ice fluff of density $\rho_\mathrm{L}$ and initial radius $r$. Determine the time after which this sphere would completely sublimate under the influence of the Sun's radiation.

Assume that the sphere considered does not heat up (the outer layers sublimate without heating the inner layers), the surface of the sphere absorbs all the radiation incident on it, and the heat of sublimation of ice is $L$. Assume also that the sphere sublimates in such a way that its shape is preserved.

In all cases (A.1, A.2 and B) give numerical values, taking $R_\mathrm{S} = 7\cdot10^{5}\,\mathrm{km}$, $T_\mathrm{S} = 5800\,\mathrm{K}$, $d = 10R_\mathrm{S}$, $C = 900\,\mathrm{J/(kg\cdot K)}$, $r = 0.4\,\mathrm{m}$, $\rho = 2.7\cdot10^{3}\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$, $\rho_\mathrm{L} = 0.5\cdot10^{3}\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$, $L = 2.7\cdot10^{6}\,\mathrm{J/kg}$.

[Formulas that may be useful (printed once for the whole paper): According to the Stefan–Boltzmann law, a perfect black body of surface area $S$ and absolute temperature $T$ emits radiation of power $P = \sigma S T^4$, where $\sigma = 5.7\cdot10^{-8}\,\mathrm{W/\left(m^2K^4\right)}$ is the Stefan–Boltzmann constant. For $|x| \ll 1$: $(1+x)^r \approx 1 + rx$, $\ln(1+x) \approx x$.]

problems.title: Problem 3
problems.problem:
Problem 3 [20 points]

Three small bodies with different masses $m_1$, $m_2$, $m_3$ are each acted on only by the forces of mutual gravitational attraction. Initially these bodies were at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side $b_0$.

a) Prove that a motion of the bodies is possible such that their mutual distances remain unchanged. Determine the angular velocity $\omega_\mathrm{r}$ of rotation of the triangle whose vertices are determined by the positions of the bodies.

b) Prove that a motion of the bodies in the plane determined by their initial positions is possible such that their mutual distances change but remain equal to one another (the triangle whose vertices are determined by the positions of the bodies is always equilateral).

c) At the initial instant the velocities of the bodies are such as if the triangle were rotating without change of size, in its own plane, with angular velocity $\omega_0$ smaller than the angular velocity $\omega_\mathrm{r}$ from part a). Calculate the minimum length of the side of the triangle $b_\mathrm{min}$ that will occur during the motion of the bodies.

problems.title: Problem 1
problems.problem:
Problem 1 [20 points]

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/poland-2021-1-fig1.png

[Label in the figure: Środek masy całego układu = centre of mass of the whole system.]

Consider an electric scooter together with the person riding on it. The total mass of the system is $M$, and the mass of the wheels and of the motor rotor can be neglected. The radius of each of the scooter's wheels is $r$, and the distance between their axles is $w$. The horizontal and vertical components of the position of the centre of mass of the scooter together with the person riding on it, measured relative to the point of contact of the rear wheel with the road, are $d$ and $h$, respectively – see the figure. The scooter has front-wheel drive, and the maximum power of its motor is $P$. The coefficient of friction between the wheels and the ground is $f$, and the road is horizontal. Assuming that the motor can work at full power at any speed, and neglecting resistance to motion, determine the minimum time of accelerating the scooter from rest to the speed $v_{\mathrm{k}}$.

Give the numerical result for $v_{\mathrm{k}} = 25\ \mathrm{km/h}$, $P = 500\ \mathrm{W}$, $M = 80\ \mathrm{kg}$, $h = 1.0\ \mathrm{m}$, $r = 0.1\ \mathrm{m}$, $w = 1.0\ \mathrm{m}$, $d = 0.5\ \mathrm{m}$, $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, $f = 0.5$.

problems.title: Problem 2
problems.problem:
Problem 2 [20 points]

A closed circular circuit (a loop) is located in a uniform magnetic field of varying induction. In the time interval $0 < t < t_0$ this induction is given by the formula

$$B(t) = B_0\left(1 - \left(\frac{t}{t_0}\right)^2\right),$$

where $B_0$ and $t_0$ are constant parameters. The loop has radius $r$ and is made of wire with resistance per unit length $\rho$. The plane of the circuit is perpendicular to the direction of the magnetic field.

Determine the minimum breaking strength $W$ of the wire such that the loop does not break in the time interval $0 < t < t_0$.

Give the numerical value of this strength for $B_0 = 4\ \mathrm{T}$, $t_0 = 0.2\ \mathrm{s}$, $r = 10\ \mathrm{cm}$, $\rho = 0.1\ \Omega/\mathrm{m}$.

Neglect the extensibility (elasticity) of the wire and assume that the induction of the magnetic field due to the current flowing in the loop is much smaller than the induction of the external field.

The breaking strength of a wire is the maximum force stretching it at which it does not break.

problems.title: Problem 3
problems.problem:
Problem 3 [20 points]

The newly founded company "On Mars you will feel lighter" plans to organise trips from a low Earth orbit to the vicinity of Mars (the clients are to cover the remaining parts of the journey by their own transport or by hiring a space taxi).

Assume that the trip can be divided into the following stages:

1. Moving away from a low (the distance from the Earth's surface is much smaller than its radius), circular Earth orbit to a relatively large distance from the Earth (such that the influence of the Earth's gravitational field can be neglected, but small compared with the Earth – Mars distance). At this stage we neglect the gravity of the Sun and take into account only the gravity of the Earth.

2. Free flight to the far surroundings of Mars (to a distance from the Sun equal to the Mars – Sun distance). At this stage we neglect the gravity of the Earth and of Mars and take into account only the gravity of the Sun. Assume that the initial velocity here is tangent to the Earth's orbit around the Sun.

The mass of the rocket not filled with fuel, but together with the cargo and the passengers, is $m_0$. The exhaust velocity of the gases from the nozzles is $v_{\mathrm{g}}$. For ecological reasons the rocket does not jettison any emptied tanks or stages. Its engine is switched on for a short time only at the beginning. While the engine is working, the influence of gravity on the motion of the rocket can be neglected.

Assume that the orbits of the Earth and of Mars, and the orbit around the Earth, are circular and lie in the same plane. A low orbit around a planet means here a circular orbit at a height small compared with the radius of that planet. The mass of the Sun is $M_{\mathrm{S}}$. The mass of the Earth, the radius of the Earth, and the distances of the centres of the Earth and of Mars from the centre of the Sun are $M_{\mathrm{Z}}$, $r_{\mathrm{Z}}$, $d_{\mathrm{Z}}$ and $d_{\mathrm{M}}$, respectively. The universal gravitational constant is $G$.

Determine the minimum mass $m_{\mathrm{p}}$ of the fuel together with the oxidiser with which the rocket must be filled in order to reach the destination of the trip. We assume that the rocket sets out on the journey at the most optimal moment (at the appropriate relative position of Mars and the Earth).

Give the numerical results taking $m_0 = 3.00\cdot10^{3}\ \mathrm{kg}$, $v_{\mathrm{g}} = 3.00\cdot10^{3}\ \mathrm{m/s}$, $M_{\mathrm{S}} = 2.00\cdot10^{30}\ \mathrm{kg}$, $M_{\mathrm{Z}} = 5.97\cdot10^{24}\ \mathrm{kg}$, $r_{\mathrm{Z}} = 6.37\cdot10^{6}\ \mathrm{m}$, $d_{\mathrm{Z}} = 1.50\cdot10^{11}\ \mathrm{m}$, $d_{\mathrm{M}} = 2.30\cdot10^{11}\ \mathrm{m}$, $G = 6.67\cdot10^{-11}\ \mathrm{m^3/(kg{\cdot}s)}$.

Information that may be useful:

The change of the rocket's velocity $\Delta v$ under the action of its engine is given by Tsiolkovsky's formula

$$\Delta v = v_{\mathrm{g}}\ln\frac{m_{\mathrm{p}}}{m_{\mathrm{k}}},$$

where $\ln$ denotes the natural logarithm (the logarithm to base $e \approx 2.718$), $m_{\mathrm{k}}$ is the total final mass, and $m_{\mathrm{p}}$ is the total initial mass.

The remark about neglecting the gravity of the Sun refers to neglecting its influence on the motion of the rocket relative to the Earth.

problems.title: Problem 1
problems.problem:
Problem 1 [20 points]

The James Webb Space Telescope orbits the Lagrange point L2 (see the definition below) along an – approximately circular – orbit of radius $r$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/poland-2022-1-fig1.png

[Labels in the figure: teleskop = telescope, Ziemia = Earth, Słońce = Sun.]

Fig. 1. Schematic representation of the Webb telescope orbiting the point L2. The Sun and the Earth are also shown.

Determine the orbital period $T$ of the telescope on this orbit, defined as the shortest time interval between two consecutive positions that correspond to the maximum distance of the telescope from the plane of the Earth's orbit around the Sun and lie on the same side of this plane. Express the result in terms of $r$, the mass of the Sun $M$, the mass of the Earth $m$, the radius of the Earth's orbit around the Sun $R$ and the period of the Earth's revolution around the Sun $T_{\mathrm{O}}$.

Neglect the interaction of the Moon and of the other celestial bodies. Assume that the Earth's orbit around the Sun is circular and take into account that the mass of the Sun is much larger than the mass of the Earth. Consider only $r$ much smaller than the distance of the Earth from the point L2.

The Lagrange point L2 is the point on the Sun–Earth axis, on the opposite side of the Earth from the Sun, such that a body placed at it can remain in the same position relative to the Sun and the Earth. Take into account that the distance of the point L2 from the centre of the Earth is much smaller than the distance of the Earth from the Sun – which follows from the fact that $M \gg m$.

Note:

Take into account that in a rotating non-inertial frame the Coriolis force acts.

The vector of this force lies in the plane of rotation of the non-inertial frame and is perpendicular to the velocity of the body in this frame. The magnitude of the Coriolis force is $2\mu\omega\,|v_{\perp}|$, where $\vec{v}_{\perp}$ is the projection of the velocity of the body onto the plane of rotation of the frame, $\omega$ – the angular velocity of this rotation, and $\mu$ – the mass of the body. The sense of this force is the same as the sense of $\vec{v}_{\perp}$ rotated by the angle $90^{\circ}$ in the plane of rotation of the frame opposite to this rotation. (Using the notion of the angular velocity vector and the vector product, the Coriolis force can be written as $-2\mu\vec{\omega}\times\vec{v}$.)

[Editorial note: the following general mathematical relations are printed at the end of the paper for all problems (the paper notes at its beginning: "Note: at the end of the text, general mathematical relations are given which may be useful in solving the problems").]

Relations that may be useful in solving the problems:

1. For $|x| \ll 1$, $(1+x)^r \approx 1 + rx$, where $r$ is a real number.

2. Relations between the speed $v$ and the distance $s$:

if $v = v_0\left(\frac{t}{t_0}\right)^n$, then $s = \frac{v_0t_0}{n+1}\left(\frac{t}{t_0}\right)^{n+1} + C$;

if $v = v_0\cos\left(\frac{t}{t_0}\right)$, then $s = v_0t_0\sin\left(\frac{t}{t_0}\right) + C$;

if $v = v_0\sin\left(\frac{t}{t_0}\right)$, then $s = -v_0t_0\cos\left(\frac{t}{t_0}\right) + C$;

if $v = v_0e^{t/t_0}$, then $s = v_0t_0e^{t/t_0} + C$;

where $t$ – time, $v_0$, $t_0$, $C$, $n$ – constants, with $n \neq -1$.

problems.title: Problem 2
problems.problem:
Problem 2 [20 points]

Inside a spherical soap bubble of radius $r_1$ there is a soap bubble of radius $r_2$ concentric with it – see the figure. The bubbles are uniformly charged – the inner one with charge $+Q$, and the outer one with charge $-Q$. The surface tension of the soapy water forming the bubbles is $\sigma$. Outside the larger bubble the air pressure is $p_0$. The system is in equilibrium. Determine the air pressure $p_2$ inside the smaller bubble and the air pressure $p_1$ between the bubbles.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/poland-2022-2-fig1.png

Fig. 2. Two concentric, charged soap bubbles.

Additional information

For soapy water with surface tension coefficient $\sigma$, the surface energy of a film of area $S$ made of it is $2\sigma S$ (the factor 2 appears because we must take into account both sides of the film).

problems.title: Problem 3
problems.problem:
Problem 3 [20 points]

A solenoid consists of $N$ uniformly wound turns of thin wire which together form the lateral surface of a cylinder of radius $r$ and length $h$, with $h \gg r$. A varying current $I = I_0\sin\Omega t$ flows through this solenoid, where $I_0$ and $\Omega$ denote positive constants, and $t$ – time. At the instant $t = 0$, through a small gap between the turns, a small ball of mass $m$, carrying charge $q$, flew into the interior of the solenoid with speed $v$, perpendicularly to its lateral surface, see Fig. 3.1.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/poland-2022-3-fig1.png

[Label in the figure: Wnętrze zwojnicy = interior of the solenoid.]

Fig. 3.1. Cross-section of the solenoid perpendicular to its axis. The ball flying into its interior is also shown.

It was observed that after a while the ball flew out of the solenoid in the direction opposite to the initial one, see Fig. 3.2.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/poland-2022-3-fig2.png

[Label in the figure: Wnętrze zwojnicy = interior of the solenoid.]

Fig. 3.2. Enlarged fragment of the cross-section of the solenoid perpendicular to its axis. Besides the ball just before entering the solenoid, the same ball just after leaving the solenoid is also shown.

a) With the other parameters fixed, determine the smallest $I_0$ for which the described situation can occur. Sketch the trajectory of the ball inside the solenoid.

b) Sketch the trajectory of the ball inside the solenoid in the following cases (a justification of each of the sketches presented is required):

(i) the value of $I_0$ is twice as large as the value determined in part a),

(ii) the value of $I_0$ is half the value determined in part a).

Assume that the distance between the place where the ball flew into the solenoid and the place where it flew out of it is much smaller than $r$ (see Fig. 3.2.) – from the point of view of the ball, it flies into a half-space filled with a magnetic field uniform in space (although varying in time). Neglect the electric field induced by the varying magnetic field and the electrostatic interaction of the ball with the wires of the solenoid.

[Editorial note: the following general mathematical relations are printed at the end of the paper for all problems (the paper notes at its beginning: "Note: at the end of the text, general mathematical relations are given which may be useful in solving the problems").]

Relations that may be useful in solving the problems:

1. For $|x| \ll 1$, $(1+x)^r \approx 1 + rx$, where $r$ is a real number.

2. Relations between the speed $v$ and the distance $s$:

if $v = v_0\left(\frac{t}{t_0}\right)^n$, then $s = \frac{v_0t_0}{n+1}\left(\frac{t}{t_0}\right)^{n+1} + C$;

if $v = v_0\cos\left(\frac{t}{t_0}\right)$, then $s = v_0t_0\sin\left(\frac{t}{t_0}\right) + C$;

if $v = v_0\sin\left(\frac{t}{t_0}\right)$, then $s = -v_0t_0\cos\left(\frac{t}{t_0}\right) + C$;

if $v = v_0e^{t/t_0}$, then $s = v_0t_0e^{t/t_0} + C$;

where $t$ – time, $v_0$, $t_0$, $C$, $n$ – constants, with $n \neq -1$.

problems.title: Problem 1
problems.problem:
Problem 1 [20 points]

A uniform ball of mass $m$ and radius $r$ was rolling without slipping with speed $v_0$ on a horizontal surface, and its axis of rotation was horizontal. At a certain moment the ball struck a smooth vertical wall at an angle $\alpha$ and bounced off it elastically. Since the wall was smooth, there was no friction between the ball and the wall. After the bounce the ball slid on the ground for some time, and the kinetic friction occurring then must be taken into account. The coefficient of this friction is $f$. The bounce off the wall lasted much shorter than the sliding of the ball after the bounce. Neglect rolling friction and air resistance.

a) Will the path of the ball after the bounce be straight, curved away from the wall, or curved towards the wall? The attached figure shows the situation from above.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/poland-2023-1-fig1.png

b) Determine the direction and the magnitude of the velocity of the ball after the sliding has stopped.

Notes:

Angular momentum is a vector, and for the ball, relative to its centre of mass, it is equal to

$$\vec{L} = I\vec{\omega},$$

where $I$ is the moment of inertia of the ball relative to the centre of mass, equal to $\frac{2}{5}mr^2$, and $\vec{\omega}$ is the angular velocity vector: its length is equal to the angular speed of rotation, its direction is the direction of the axis of rotation, and its sense is given by the right-hand screw rule.

Newton's second law for rotational motion has the form

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}\vec{L}}{\mathrm{d}t} = \vec{M},$$

where $\vec{M}$ is the resultant torque; in the case of many forces $\vec{F}_i$ acting on a given object it is equal to

$$\vec{M} = \sum_i \vec{r}_i\times\vec{F}_i,$$

where $\vec{r}_i$ is the vector starting at the point relative to which we calculate $\vec{M}$ and ending at the point of application of the force $\vec{F}_i$.

Above, $\times$ is the vector product; we have: $\left|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}\right| = |\vec{a}|\cdot\left|\vec{b}\right|\,|\sin\theta|$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$; the vector $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$, and its sense is given by the right-hand screw rule (we rotate from $\vec{a}$ to $\vec{b}$). The usual rule for differentiating a product holds for the vector product: $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(\vec{a}\times\vec{b}\right) = \frac{\mathrm{d}\vec{a}}{\mathrm{d}t}\times\vec{b} + \vec{a}\times\frac{\mathrm{d}\vec{b}}{\mathrm{d}t}$

problems.title: Problem 2
problems.problem:
Problem 2 [20 points]

Consider the following model of an underwater geyser.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/poland-2023-2-fig1.png

At a depth $h$ below the surface of a very shallow lake, in the rocks, there is a cave (a reservoir) completely filled with water. The rocks surrounding the reservoir have temperature $T_{\mathrm{s}}$. These rocks heat the water in the reservoir and at a certain moment it begins to boil. The water vapour completely pushes the water out of the channel connecting the cave with the lake, and then a sudden evaporation of part of the water in the reservoir occurs, visible as an eruption of the geyser.

The air pressure just above the surface of the lake is $p_0$, and the temperature of the water in the lake is $T_{\mathrm{j}}$. The height of the reservoir is much smaller than $h$. The volume of the channel connecting the cave with the lake is negligibly small compared with the volume of the reservoir, but it is wide enough not to resist the escaping vapour. During the eruption, water from the lake does not flow into the channel. Take into account that the density of the vapour is much smaller than the density of water. Assume that only vapour escapes from the geyser.

a) What must the temperature $T_{\mathrm{s}}$ be for the described phenomenon to be able to occur?

b) Assuming that during the eruption of the geyser a mass $m$ of water vapour escapes from it, determine the minimum amount of water accumulated in the cave under consideration just before the eruption of the geyser.

Neglect the heat supplied to the water during the eruption.

c) After the eruption the pressure in the reservoir drops and the water from the lake fills the reservoir again. Knowing that the time interval between eruptions is $\Delta t$, determine the average power of the heat supplied to the water.

The pressure of saturated vapour at temperature $T$ is, in the situation under consideration, to a good approximation equal to

$$p_{\mathrm{w}}(T) = p_0\,\mathrm{e}^{\frac{L_{\mathrm{m}}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_0}-\frac{1}{T}\right)},$$

where $R$ is the universal gas constant, $L_{\mathrm{m}}$ the molar heat of vaporisation of water at pressure $p_0$, and $T_0$ the boiling point of water at pressure $p_0$. Assume that the density of water does not depend on temperature and is equal to $\rho$. Assume also that the specific heat of water does not depend on temperature (in the range of temperatures occurring) and is equal to $c_{\mathrm{w}}$.

The molar mass of water is $M_{\mathrm{w}}$, the gravitational acceleration $g$.

Give the numerical results taking $h = 200\ \mathrm{m}$, $L_{\mathrm{m}} = 41\ \mathrm{kJ/mol}$, $T_0 = 373\ \mathrm{K}$, $R = 8.3\ \mathrm{J/mol{\cdot}K}$, $c_{\mathrm{w}} = 4.2\ \mathrm{kJ/(kg{\cdot}K)}$, $M_{\mathrm{w}} = 18\ \mathrm{g/mol}$, $g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, $\rho = 1000\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$, $m = 50\cdot10^{3}\ \mathrm{kg}$, $\Delta t = 1\ \mathrm{h}$, $T_{\mathrm{j}} = 293\ \mathrm{K}$, $p_0 = 1000\ \mathrm{hPa}$.

problems.title: Problem 3
problems.problem:
Problem 3 [20 points]

Two metal balls, each of radius $r$, are immersed in a large tank of salt water with conductivity $\sigma$ and permittivity $\epsilon$. The balls are connected to a battery by thin insulated wires, and their centres are a distance $d$ apart – see the figure. The voltage between them is $U$.

Assuming that the electric field outside the balls is the same as the field of point charges located at the centres of these balls, determine the current flowing through the water. Present the result to an accuracy of terms linear in $\frac{r}{d}$, i.e. in the form $A(1 + B\frac{r}{d})$, where $A$ and $B$ do not depend on $\frac{r}{d}$; this means neglecting terms of order $\frac{r^2}{d^2}$.

Give the numerical result for $U = 5\ \mathrm{V}$, $d = 0.1\ \mathrm{m}$, $r = 0.01\ \mathrm{m}$, $\sigma = 10^{-2}\ 1/(\Omega\cdot\mathrm{cm}) = 1.0\ /(\Omega\cdot\mathrm{m})$ $\epsilon = \epsilon_w\cdot\epsilon_0$ where $\epsilon_w = 80$, $\epsilon_0 = 8.85\cdot10^{-12}\ \mathrm{A^2{\cdot}s^4/(kg\cdot m^3)}$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/poland-2023-3-fig1.png

Notes:

1. The electric field due to a point charge $q$ located in a uniform medium of permittivity $\epsilon$ is given by the formula

$$\vec{E}(\vec{r}) = \frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon r^2}\,\frac{\vec{r}}{r},$$

where $\vec{r}$ is the vector from the charge to the point at which we examine the electric field.

2. The current density (i.e. the current per unit area) in a medium of conductivity $\sigma$, at a point where the electric field is $\vec{E}$, is equal to $\sigma\vec{E}$. This means that the current flowing through a small surface element $A$, perpendicular to $\vec{E}$, is equal to $\sigma AE$.

3. The walls and the surface of the water in the tank are at a much greater distance from the balls than the distance between them.

4. The electric field due to the wires can be neglected (this follows from the fact that they are thin).

5. For $|x| < 1$ the following holds:

$$(1+x)^{\alpha} = 1 + \frac{\alpha}{1!}x + \frac{\alpha(\alpha-1)}{2!}x^2 + \ldots$$

problems.title: Problem 1
problems.problem:
Problem 1 [20 points]

Inside a rectangular-cuboid tank with a flat horizontal bottom and width $L$, a uniform dam in the shape of a quarter-cylinder of radius $R$ and length $L$ has been placed along the side of width $L$ – see the figure. The depth of the water in the tank is also $R$ – see the figure:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/poland-2024-1-fig1.png

The dam is not fastened in any way – neither to the bottom nor at its ends, but the coefficient of friction between the material of the dam and the ground is non-zero and equal to $f$.

Find the minimum mass $m$ of the dam for which the water will neither shift it nor overturn it. The density of water is $\rho$, the gravitational acceleration is $g$.

We assume that the water does not seep under the base of the dam, but also that the dam does not stick to the ground by suction.

problems.title: Problem 2
problems.problem:
Problem 2 [20 points]

A solenoid has $N$ uniformly and densely wound turns, length $L$ and radius $r$, where $L\gg r$. In a plane perpendicular to the axis of the solenoid there is a non-conducting, uniform ring of inner radius $R_1$, outer radius $R_2$ ($L\gg R_2>R_1>r$) and mass $m$. The ring is equidistant from the ends of the solenoid, is uniformly charged with charge $Q$ and can rotate freely about its axis, which coincides with the axis of the solenoid.

At the instant $t=0$ the ring is not rotating. Find the angular velocity of rotation of the ring at the instant $t=T$, if a time-dependent current $I(t)=I_0\cdot t/T$ flows through the solenoid, where $I_0$ is a constant.

Neglect the magnetic field produced by the ring and the electrostatic charge induced by it in the circuit of the solenoid. Assume that the system is in vacuum.

The moment of inertia of a uniform disc of mass $M$ and radius $R$ about its axis is $MR^2/2$.

problems.title: Problem 3
problems.problem:
Problem 3 [20 points]

The newly founded company "Relax on your way to Mars" intends to produce recreational modules for spacecraft.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/poland-2024-3-fig1.png

Diagram of the module. The water stream is shown in the frame co-rotating with the module.

[Labels in the figure: wewnętrzna powierzchnia modułu = inner surface of the module; kierunek obrotu modułu = direction of rotation of the module; woda = water; oś obrotu = axis of rotation; strumień wody ze zraszacza = water stream from the sprinkler.]

Such a module has the shape of a hollow cylinder of inner radius $R$. During the journey, when the rocket engines are switched off, the cylinder rotates about its axis at such a rate that the effective gravitational acceleration on the inner surface equals $g$. This inner surface is covered with a thin layer of soil on which grass grows. The grass is watered by sprinklers placed at ground level, fed from a water tank located on the axis of rotation. The air pressure inside the module and in the very small space "above" the water (i.e. right next to the axis of rotation) is equal to the Earth's atmospheric pressure $p_0$. The only cause of the flow of water to the sprinkler, and then of its outflow from it, is the "artificial gravity" caused by the rotational motion of the module.

Consider a stream of water emerging in the plane perpendicular to the axis of rotation at an angle $\alpha$ with respect to the ground, where $\alpha=0$ means outflow of the water in the direction of rotation of the cylinder. We assume that just past the outlet of the opening, all volume elements of the water move with the same velocity and in the same direction.

Assuming that there are no energy losses – neither during the flow of the water to the sprinkler nor after the water leaves the sprinkler – find the distance (measured along the inner surface of the cylinder) and the maximum height (measured as the distance along the radius from the ground) reached by the considered stream of water. Assume also that the speed of the water flow in the pipes connecting the tank with the sprinkler is much smaller than the speed of the water flowing out of the sprinkler. The mass of the outflowing water is much smaller than the mass of the station.

problems.title: Problem 1
problems.problem:
Problem 1 [20 points]

A space station orbits a certain spherical dwarf planet of mass $M$ along an elliptical orbit with pericentre $r_{\mathrm{p}}$ and apocentre $r_{\mathrm{a}}$. The station consists of two modules: 1 (of mass $m_1$) and 2 (of mass $m_2$), the astronauts being in module 1 (their mass is included in the mass of this module). The crew of the station has mutinied, and its aim is to eject module 2 in such a way that module 1, which they occupy, moves away from the planet beyond the practical range of its gravitational field (formally – to an infinitely large distance, of course over a very long time). The modules are separated by the explosion of charges located between them. The energy of the explosion is $E_{\mathrm{w}}$, and half of this energy is converted into the kinetic energy of the modules.

Find the minimum value of the energy $E_{\mathrm{w}}$ that makes the described manoeuvre possible. Assume that the direction in which module 2 is ejected can be controlled arbitrarily, and moreover that the ejection can take place at any point of the orbit. The duration of the ejection of the module is so short that during the ejection the influence of the gravity of the planet can be neglected, but long enough that the astronauts come to no harm from the action of a large g-force. The mutual gravitational interaction of the modules and the gravitational field produced by other celestial bodies should be neglected. Neglect the mass of the explosive charges compared with the masses of the modules. Neither the station as a whole nor the modules after separation rotate.

Give the numerical result when this dwarf planet is Ceres of mass $M=9.4\cdot10^{20}\,\mathrm{kg}$, and $m_1=1.0\cdot10^{5}\,\mathrm{kg}$, $m_2=4.0\cdot10^{5}\,\mathrm{kg}$, $r_{\mathrm{p}}=1.0\cdot10^{6}\,\mathrm{m}$, $r_{\mathrm{a}}=5.0\cdot10^{6}\,\mathrm{m}$. The gravitational constant is $G=6.67\cdot10^{-11}\,\mathrm{N\cdot m^2/kg^2}$.

problems.title: Problem 2
problems.problem:
Problem 2 [20 points]

A driver was driving a car at night along a straight road. At a certain moment he heard a short sound signal of frequency $f$, coming from a direction making an angle $\alpha$ with the direction of travel. The driver immediately strained his eyes and saw straight ahead (along the road) the lights of a locomotive passing over a level crossing. The driver knows that in this area the railway track is perpendicular to the road, the trains here travel at constant speed, and the locomotives emit a sound signal of frequency $f_0$. He also knows that the speed of sound in air is $v_{\mathrm{d}}$.

The driver immediately began to brake, moving with uniformly decelerated motion with an acceleration of magnitude $a$, as a result of which he stopped just in front of the tracks.

Find the distance of the locomotive from the car at the moment the car stops.

Give the numerical result for $\alpha=10^{\circ}$, $f_0=400\,\mathrm{Hz}$, $f=460\,\mathrm{Hz}$, $v_{\mathrm{d}}=340\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $a=5\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

Neglect the linear dimensions of the locomotive and of the car. The day was windless and the area flat.

problems.title: Problem 3
problems.problem:
Problem 3 [20 points]

A very long (i.e. of length much greater than its radius), uniform, rigid, hollow tube with thin walls and radius $R$ lies on a horizontal ground. The tube is cut by a horizontal plane parallel to the plane of the ground, at such a distance from it that the surface of the upper part of the tube is a fraction $x$ of the whole surface of the tube. A uniform current of total intensity $I$ flows through the upper part of the tube, along its axis, and a uniform current of total intensity $-I$ through the lower part. The mass of the tube per unit length is $\lambda$. Find the minimum current $I_{\min}$ above which the upper part of the tube will rise above the lower part.

Neglect the forces associated with the connecting wires. The gravitational acceleration is $g$, and the magnetic permeability of vacuum is $\mu_0$.

problems.title: Problem 1
problems.problem:
Problem 1 [20 points]

A uniform ball of mass $M$ and radius $r$ rests on a flat, horizontal ground. A small ball of mass $m$ and negligibly small radius is dropped onto the ball. The velocity of the small ball just before the collision is vertical and has magnitude $v_0$; the collision takes place at height $h$ above the ground ($h>r$). We consider only the situation in which, after the collision, the small ball rises, its maximum height during the motion being $H$ ($H>h$) above the ground.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/poland-2026-1-fig1.png

Find the velocity of the centre of the large ball after the collision. Give the numerical result for $r=8\,\mathrm{cm}$, $h=15\,\mathrm{cm}$, $H=20\,\mathrm{cm}$, $M=3\,\mathrm{kg}$, $m=0.2\,\mathrm{kg}$, $v_0=5\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and the gravitational acceleration $g=9.81\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

Assume that the collision between the balls lasts a very short time, the surfaces of the balls are smooth, and the friction between them is zero. The coefficient of friction between the large ball and the ground is so large that this ball does not slip on the ground either during the collision or after it. Moreover, the large ball is in contact with the ground all the time; it does not bounce off it. There is no air resistance. The moment of inertia of a uniform ball about an axis through its centre is $I=2Mr^2/5$.

Note: it cannot be assumed that the collision is elastic.

problems.title: Problem 2
problems.problem:
Problem 2 [20 points]

A spherical planetoid of radius $R$ has been discovered in which, under a very thin rocky surface, there is an incompressible liquid of density $\rho$, and at the centre there is a spherical, spherically symmetric rocky core of radius $r_1$. A spherical probe of mass $m$ was immersed in the liquid to the maximum possible depth, i.e. down to the rocky core; the pressure measured by the probe at this depth is $p_1$. The dependence of the volume of the probe on the pressure $p$ is given by the formula $V=V_0(1-\alpha p)$, where $V_0$ and $\alpha$ are positive constants.

a) Find the minimum work that must be done in pulling the probe out of the liquid filling the planetoid by means of a weightless, thin, flexible and inextensible rope.

b) Find the mass of the rocky core.

The volume and the mass of the probe are much smaller than, respectively, the volume and the mass of the liquid. Neglect the gravity of other celestial bodies. The pressure at the surface of the liquid, i.e. just below the rocky layer, is much smaller than $p_1$ (practically equal to 0) and does not change while the probe is being pulled out.

In cases a) and b) find the numerical results for $R=4.00\cdot10^{5}\,\mathrm{m}$, $r_1=2.00\cdot10^{5}\,\mathrm{m}$, $p_1=3.00\cdot10^{7}\,\mathrm{Pa}$, $\rho=1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$, $m=10\,\mathrm{kg}$, $V_0=1.05\cdot10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m^3}$, $\alpha=6.00\cdot10^{-9}\,/\mathrm{Pa}$. The gravitational constant is $G=6.67\cdot10^{-11}\,\mathrm{m^3/(kg\cdot s^2)}$.

problems.title: Problem 3
problems.problem:
Problem 3 [20 points]

Consider $N$ rigid, thin, long wires, parallel to one another, which – when no current flows – form the $N$ lateral edges of a regular prism. The distance between neighbouring edges is $d$, see the figure (it corresponds to the special case $N=6$). A current $I_k=I_0\cos(\omega t+2k\pi/N)$ flows through wire $k$ (where $k=1,2,\ \ldots,N$), where $I_0$ (the current amplitude) and $\omega$ (the angular frequency) are constants and $t$ is time.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/poland-2026-3-fig1.png

The wires are mounted elastically, so that they can be displaced radially (change their distance from the axis of the prism), but they cannot move in the direction perpendicular to the radial one. Displacing a wire from the edge of the prism by a distance $x$ requires a force $Kx$ per unit length of the wire, where $K$ is a constant. The mass of each wire per unit length is $\lambda$.

a) For what angular frequency $\omega$ does resonance occur?

b) Assuming that there is no resonance, find the mean radial displacement from the edge of the prism and the amplitude of the radial oscillations of each of the wires a long time after the current is switched on. Take a positive value of this displacement to correspond to an increase of the distance of the wire from the axis of the prism.

Assume that the displacement of a wire from the edge of the prism is small compared with $d$ – so small that even in the case of resonance this displacement does not affect the forces of mutual interaction of the wires.

Notes:

If a periodic force $F=F_0\cos(\Omega t)$ acts on a harmonic oscillator of mass $m$ and spring constant $k$, then after a long time, for $\Omega^2\neq k/m$, the oscillator will oscillate according to the formula $x=A\cos(\Omega t)$, where $A=F_0/(k-m\Omega^2)$ (these are the so-called steady-state oscillations).

Note that the quantity $I_0\cos(\omega t+\alpha)$ can be interpreted as the $x$-component of a vector of length $I_0$ rotating in the $xy$ plane with angular velocity $\omega$, where at the instant $t=0$ this vector makes an angle $\alpha$ with the $x$ axis.

Assume that the magnetic interactions are as if the system were in vacuum. Neglect the influence of the supply wires – those bringing the current in and taking it out (they are not shown in the figure; the mountings of the wires are not shown either).
